headline: Two weeks, 50 hours of overtime. No climate deal.
summary: UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended Sunday without an agreement, more than 50 hours past the deadline. The fight was over whether the text would mention fossil fuels. Russia and Saudi Arabia wanted them out. The EU and Pacific island states refused to sign without them. Smaller deals passed. The rest waits for Ethiopia next year.

cover_question.q: How can one country block it?

cover_answer: Deals need consensus. A few countries saying no is enough.
table_question: Would you sign a deal you thought was too weak, or walk away?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Grown-ups from almost every country sat in one big room in Turkey for two weeks to agree on how to keep the Earth from getting too hot. The rule there is that everyone has to say yes, like a game that only starts when every kid agrees. Some countries said no, so they went home without a plan. They will try again next year.
5-7.why: One room, one rule, everyone has to say yes. A six-year-old knows that game, and the rule carries the story.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, and a game that only starts when every kid says yes is a scene they have lived. The script has no vivid image to frighten them, only the rule and the grown-ups coming back next year. Expect 'is the Earth going to be OK?' It is getting warmer, and a lot of adults are working on it.

8-12.script: Burning coal, oil and gas heats the planet, so most countries wanted the deal to say the world should move away from them. Russia and Saudi Arabia wanted those words out. These talks work like a class rule that only counts if everyone agrees, so two extra days ended with no deal at all.
8-12.why: Burning fuel warms the planet, the rule says everyone must agree, and two countries wouldn't. That chain is one they can follow.
8-12.why_long: At ten the question underneath is fairness: how can a few countries overrule a hundred? The script hands them the chain, from burning fuel to a consensus rule to two refusals, and the class rule is one they have sat through. Expect 'why don't they change the rule?' The countries that like it would have to agree to that too.

13-17.script: Is a weak deal better than no deal? Palau said yes and would have signed. The EU and the Marshall Islands said no, and 50 hours of overtime ended with nothing. Palau's minister says the smaller deals that passed mean it was not a failure. Second: when would you walk away from a bad compromise?
13-17.why: Palau and the Marshall Islands are both small island nations, and they split on the same text. That is the argument worth having.
13-17.why_long: A thirteen-year-old can hold two true things at once: the deal was weak, and no deal may be worse. Palau and the Marshall Islands read the same text and split, a real disagreement to test. Expect 'so is it hopeless?' No. Bowen says the move off fossil fuels is happening anyway. The fight was over writing it down.

5-7.a: They fought over whether the plan should name coal, oil and gas.

8-12.q: Why did they need everyone to agree?
8-12.a: That's the rule here. Any country can say no, and the EU did.

8-12.q: So did two weeks get nothing done?
8-12.a: Not nothing. Nearly 100 countries pledged to use more electricity.

13-17.q: How can one country block it?
13-17.a: Deals need consensus. The EU and a few others refused the text.

13-17.q: Does it matter if the text names fossil fuels?
13-17.a: Two extra days of talks went on it. The 2023 Dubai pledge stands.
